blocks.text: Richard was a little late in the morning, but I did not have to wait long for him. We turned into the park. The air was bright and wet with morning dew, and there was not a cloud in the sky. The birds sang, and it was a joy to hear them. Tiny points of light shone in the fern, the grass, and the trees, and they were extremely beautiful to see. The woods seemed to have grown twenty times richer since yesterday. During the quiet night, they had looked so huge and silent in sleep. Yet it seemed as if, during that night, Nature had been more awake than usual. That seemed true through all the tiny details of every wonderful leaf, for the grand beauty of that day.
“This is a lovely place,” said Richard, looking around. “There is none of the harshness and disagreement of court cases here!”
But there was other trouble.
“I tell you what, my dear girl,” said Richard. “When I get matters in general settled, I think I will come down here and rest.”
“Would it not be better to rest now?” I asked.
“Oh, when it comes to resting now,” said Richard, “or doing anything very clear and settled now, that's not easy. In short, it can't be done. At least, I can't do it.”
“Why not?” said I.

“You know why not, Esther. Suppose you were living in an unfinished house. Its roof could be put on or taken off, or the house could be pulled down or built up from top to bottom. That might happen tomorrow, the next day, next week, next month, or next year. In such a place, you would find it hard to rest or settle. So do I. Now? There's no ‘now’ for those of us who have a case in court.”

When I saw the darkened look from last night again, I could almost have believed in the attraction that my poor little wandering friend had talked about at great length. That look also had in it a slight trace of that unfortunate man who had died. This was terrible to think about.
“My dear Richard,” said I, “this is a bad beginning of our conversation.”
“I knew you would tell me so, Dame Durden.”
“And I am not the only one, dear Richard. I was not the one who warned you once never to build a hope or expectation on the family curse.”

“There you come back to John Jarndyce!” said Richard impatiently. “Well! We must talk about him sooner or later, because he is the main part of what I have to say. So it is just as good to do it right now. My dear Esther, how can you be so blind? Don't you see that he is one of the people in the court case, with his own interests in it? It may be very good for him to want me to know nothing about the case and care nothing about it. But don't you see that it may not be quite so good for me?”

“Oh, Richard,” I protested, “is such a thing possible? You have seen him and heard him, and you have lived under his roof and known him. How can you ever have done all that, and still say even a word of such shameful suspicions? How can you speak of them even to me, in this lonely place where there is no one to hear us?”
His face turned deep red, as if the naturally generous part of him felt a sudden, sharp sting of blame. He was silent for a little while, before he replied in a low, quiet voice:
“Esther, I am sure you know that I am not a low, small-minded man. And I am sure you know I have some understanding that suspicion and lack of trust are bad qualities in someone of my age.”
“I know it very well,” I said. “There is nothing that I am more sure of.”

“You're a dear girl!” replied Richard. “And that is just like you, because it gives me comfort. I really need to get some small bit of comfort out of all this business, because even at its best it is a bad one. I do not need to tell you that.”

“I know perfectly well,” I said. “I know just as well, Richard—what shall I say?—just as well as you do, that putting such a wrong meaning on things does not belong to your nature at all. And I know, just as well as you know, what changes your nature so much.”

“Come, sister, come,” said Richard, a little more cheerfully. “You will be fair with me, in any case. If I have the bad luck to be under that influence, so does he. If it has twisted me a little, it may have twisted him a little, too. I am not denying that he is a man of honor, outside of all these complicated matters and all this uncertainty. I am sure he is. But it spoils something in everybody. You know it spoils something in everybody. You have heard him say so fifty times. Then why should he escape?”
